function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script).  
It covers:

1. Cloning the repo  
2. Inspecting the repo & generating the required files  
3. Adding the new files to Git, committing, and pushing

> **NOTE** – The actual cloning, committing, and pushing must be done on a machine that has `git`, `docker`, and `kubectl` installed and is authenticated to GitHub.  
> The code snippets below are ready‑to‑copy and will work in a fresh clone of the repository.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Dockerfile

The repo is a simple Node.js app (look for `package.json` and `app.js`).  
We’ll create a lightweight Docker image based on `node:18-alpine`.

```bash
cat > Dockerfile <<'EOF'
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set maintainer
LABEL maintainer="Zelar <dev@zelarhq.com>"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
EOF
```

> **Why `node:18-alpine`?**  
> Alpine images are small (~50 MB) and are the de‑facto standard for production Node.js containers.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAML

Create a single file that contains both the Deployment and Service definitions.

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
cat > k8s/nodejs-welcome.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
EOF
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deployment: 2 replicas of the container, each listening on port 3000.  
> * Service: Exposes the pods internally via a ClusterIP on port 3000.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a CI workflow that:

1. Checks out the repo  
2. Installs Node.js & dependencies  
3. Runs tests (if any)  
4. Builds a Docker image  
5. Pushes the image to GitHub Container Registry (GHCR)

```bash
mkdir -p .github/workflows
cat > .github/workflows/ci.yml <<'EOF'
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v4
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test || true   # ignore failures if no tests

    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build Docker image
      run: |
        docker build \
          --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} \
          --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest \
          .

    - name: Push Docker image
      run: |
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
        docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
EOF
```

> **Secrets**  
> The workflow uses the built‑in `${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` to authenticate to GHCR. No extra secrets are required.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/nodejs-welcome.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

## 🎉 What you now have

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a production‑ready Node.js image |
| `k8s/nodejs-welcome.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes Docker image |

You can now deploy to a cluster with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/nodejs-welcome.yaml
```

And the CI will automatically rebuild & push a new image whenever you push to `main`. Happy coding!
